questions.question: What is Git?
questions.correctAnswer: A distributed version control system that records the history of code changes.
wrongAnswers: A centralized version control system that stores the full history only on a central server and requires a network connection for every commit.
A hosting platform that stores repositories in the cloud and provides pull requests, issues and continuous integration pipelines.
A package manager for installing JavaScript libraries.

questions.question: What is GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: A Git repository hosting platform with collaboration features: pull requests, issues, Actions, projects and code review.
wrongAnswers: The official command-line implementation of Git, maintained by Linus Torvalds, used to create commits, branches and merges locally on your machine.
An open source version control system that replaces Git with a centralized model, focused on large enterprises and binary files.
The official command-line tool that implements Git.

questions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: Git is the local versioning tool; GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration.
wrongAnswers: GitHub is the local command-line versioning tool, while Git is the online service that hosts repositories and adds pull requests and issues.
Git is the paid version of GitHub with extra features.
GitHub is the local tool; Git is the online hosting service.

questions.question: What is a repository?
questions.correctAnswer: A project folder with the entire version history and Git configuration.
wrongAnswers: A single commit containing all project files.
A remote server that only stores the latest version of the code.
A list of the project's npm dependencies.

questions.question: What is a commit?
questions.correctAnswer: A "snapshot" of changes, with author, date, message and a unique hash.
wrongAnswers: A request to merge one branch into another.
A copy of a repository in your own account.
A pointer to the current branch.

questions.question: What is a branch?
questions.correctAnswer: An independent line of development, a movable pointer to a commit.
wrongAnswers: A full copy of the repository stored in a separate folder on disk, including its own history and configuration files.
A fixed, immutable label attached to a specific commit, commonly used to mark release versions such as v1.0.0.
A fixed label for a release version, like v1.0.0.

questions.question: How do you clone a repository?
questions.correctAnswer: git clone <url>.
wrongAnswers: git fork <url>, which copies the remote repository into your account.
git checkout <url> --clone to download all branches.
git pull <url> --new.

questions.question: How do you create a new branch and switch to it?
questions.correctAnswer: git switch -c branch-name (or git checkout -b branch-name).
wrongAnswers: git checkout branch-name --new, which creates the branch from main and moves HEAD.
git branch -m branch-name.
git switch branch-name --create-only.

questions.question: What does git add do?
questions.correctAnswer: It adds changes to the staging area for the next commit.
wrongAnswers: It creates a new commit containing every modified file in the working directory, using a default message.
It registers a new remote URL in the repository configuration so you can push to it later.
It creates a new commit with all modified files.

questions.question: What does git commit -m do?
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a commit with the staged changes and the given message.
wrongAnswers: It merges the current branch into main with a message.
It edits the message of the last pushed commit.
It sends a message to the repository's collaborators.

questions.question: What does git push do?
questions.correctAnswer: It sends local commits to the remote repository.
wrongAnswers: It downloads new commits from the remote repository and merges them into the current branch.
It saves uncommitted changes temporarily so you can switch branches with a clean working directory.
It creates a pull request automatically.

questions.question: What does git pull do?
questions.correctAnswer: It fetches changes from the remote and integrates them into the current branch (fetch + merge, or rebase if configured).
wrongAnswers: It uploads your local commits to the remote repository and opens a pull request automatically on GitHub.
It only downloads changes without modifying the current branch.
It sends local commits to the remote.

questions.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
questions.correctAnswer: fetch only downloads updates without changing your branch; pull downloads and integrates.
wrongAnswers: pull only downloads remote updates without changing your branch, while fetch downloads and integrates them through a merge or rebase.
fetch works only with GitHub remotes and requires authentication, while pull works with any remote and accepts anonymous access.
pull only downloads; fetch downloads and merges.

questions.question: What is a fork?
questions.correctAnswer: A copy of a repository into your account, used to contribute to third-party projects.
wrongAnswers: A new branch created inside the original repository, used by maintainers to work on features in isolation.
A merge conflict between two branches.
A tag that marks a stable version.

questions.question: What is a Pull Request (PR)?
questions.correctAnswer: A request to merge changes from one branch into another, allowing review, discussion and automated checks.
wrongAnswers: A command that pulls the latest changes from the remote.
A request to gain write access to a repository.
A request to download a repository as a ZIP file.

questions.question: What is an Issue?
questions.correctAnswer: A record for tracking bugs, tasks, ideas and discussions in a repository.
wrongAnswers: An automatic error report that GitHub generates whenever a commit fails to build or a test fails in CI.
A pull request that has been blocked by branch protection and is waiting for administrator approval.
A security alert generated by Dependabot only.

questions.question: What is .gitignore?
questions.correctAnswer: A file listing patterns of files and folders that Git should ignore (e.g., node_modules, .env).
wrongAnswers: A file that lists collaborators who are not allowed to push to the repository, enforced by GitHub on every push.
A file that hides commits from the history.
A file that deletes listed files from the remote.

questions.question: What is README.md?
questions.correctAnswer: The project's presentation document, displayed on the repository's home page.
wrongAnswers: A file that configures GitHub Actions workflows, listing the jobs that run on each push and pull request.
The changelog that Git generates automatically from commit messages every time a new tag is created.
A file that Git reads to set default branch names.

questions.question: What is origin?
questions.correctAnswer: The default name of the remote repository you cloned from.
wrongAnswers: The default name of the main branch in every new repository, replacing the older master name.
The very first commit in the repository's history, from which all other commits descend.
The original author of the repository.

questions.question: How do you view the commit history?
questions.correctAnswer: git log (or git log --oneline --graph).
wrongAnswers: git history --all, which lists commits from every branch.
git history.
git status --all.

questions.question: How do you view the state of files?
questions.correctAnswer: git status.
wrongAnswers: git log --files, listing changed files.
git diff --status for each file.
git log --files.

questions.question: How do you view differences in changes?
questions.correctAnswer: git diff (unstaged) and git diff --staged (staged).
wrongAnswers: git compare for unstaged changes and git compare --cached for staged changes.
git status -v for unstaged changes and git status -vv for staged changes.
git log -p only, which shows staged changes.

questions.question: What is HEAD?
questions.correctAnswer: A pointer to the current commit you are on (usually the tip of the active branch).
wrongAnswers: A pointer to the latest commit on the remote main branch, updated every time someone pushes to the repository.
The first commit of the repository, used as the root from which all branches are created.
The repository's main configuration file.

questions.question: What is the main branch?
questions.correctAnswer: The current default main branch of repositories (formerly commonly called master).
wrongAnswers: A protected branch that can only be modified by GitHub administrators.
A branch automatically created for each release.
The branch where GitHub stores pull request drafts.

questions.question: How do you discard uncommitted changes in a file?
questions.correctAnswer: git restore <file> (formerly git checkout -- file).
wrongAnswers: git revert <file>, which creates a new commit undoing the changes in that file.
git reset --soft <file>, which discards local edits but keeps them staged.
git reset --soft <file>.

questions.question: How do you remove a file from staging?
questions.correctAnswer: git restore --staged <file>.
wrongAnswers: git rm <file>, which unstages it and keeps the file on disk.
git unstage --all <file>.
git reset --hard <file>.

questions.question: How do you change the last commit message?
questions.correctAnswer: git commit --amend (avoid it if you already pushed to a shared branch).
wrongAnswers: git commit --edit-last, which rewrites only the message and is always safe on shared branches that others already pulled.
git revert --message, which creates a new commit replacing the previous message without rewriting any history.
git rename HEAD.

questions.question: What is a tag?
questions.correctAnswer: A marker for a specific commit, commonly used for versions such as v1.0.0.
wrongAnswers: A movable pointer that advances automatically with each new commit, used to track release lines such as v1.x.
A label applied to issues to categorize them.
A movable pointer that follows new commits, like a branch.

questions.question: What is a Release on GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: A tag-based version publication, with notes and attached files.
wrongAnswers: An automatic deployment of the main branch to production triggered whenever a pull request is merged.
A merged pull request that received at least two approvals and is therefore marked as releasable.
A merged pull request with more than one approval.

questions.question: What is GitHub Pages?
questions.correctAnswer: A free service to host static sites directly from a repository.
wrongAnswers: A wiki for documenting repositories, not for hosting sites.
A paid service for hosting Node.js backends.
A page listing all public repositories of a user.

questions.question: How do you authenticate with GitHub via the terminal?
questions.correctAnswer: With SSH keys, Personal Access Tokens or GitHub CLI (gh auth login); passwords are no longer accepted.
wrongAnswers: With your GitHub account password, which remains the recommended method for HTTPS remotes in the terminal.
With your email address only, since GitHub identifies terminal users by the email configured in git config.
With an OAuth app secret stored in .gitignore.

questions.question: What is the GitHub CLI (gh)?
questions.correctAnswer: A command-line tool to create PRs, issues and manage repositories without leaving the terminal.
wrongAnswers: The official Git implementation maintained by GitHub, which replaces the git command for every version control operation.
A graphical desktop client for Git.
A CI runner that executes Actions locally.

questions.question: What are public and private repositories?
questions.correctAnswer: Public can be seen by anyone; private only by authorized people.
wrongAnswers: Public repositories can be edited by anyone with a GitHub account; private repositories can be viewed by anyone but only edited by the owner.
Public repositories are always free and hosted on GitHub, while private repositories must be hosted on your own servers.
Public are free and private are always paid, regardless of features.

questions.question: What is an open source license?
questions.correctAnswer: A document (MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL...) that defines how third parties may use, modify and distribute the code.
wrongAnswers: A paid certificate issued by GitHub proving that the code has been audited and is free of security vulnerabilities and bugs.
A repository setting that makes the code public and automatically allows anyone to push changes without review.
A key required to install open source packages.

questions.question: What is the difference between merge and rebase?
questions.correctAnswer: merge joins histories by creating a merge commit; rebase reapplies commits onto another base, producing a linear history but rewriting it.
wrongAnswers: rebase joins histories by creating a merge commit that preserves both lines; merge reapplies commits onto a new base and rewrites them linearly.
rebase creates a merge commit; merge rewrites history linearly.
merge deletes the source branch; rebase keeps it.

questions.question: When should you not use rebase?
questions.correctAnswer: On public/shared branches, because it rewrites history and causes problems for other collaborators.
wrongAnswers: On local branches that have never been pushed.
When the branch has fewer than five commits.
Whenever there are no conflicts, since rebase only works with conflicts.

questions.question: What is "squash and merge"?
questions.correctAnswer: A GitHub option that combines all of a PR's commits into a single commit on the target branch.
wrongAnswers: A GitHub option that merges the pull request while keeping every individual commit and adding an extra merge commit on top.
An option that deletes all commits of the PR without merging.
An option that compresses repository files to save space.

questions.question: What is git stash?
questions.correctAnswer: It temporarily stores uncommitted changes to clean the working directory; git stash pop restores them.
wrongAnswers: It creates a new branch from the uncommitted changes, commits them and pushes the branch to the remote as a backup copy.
It permanently deletes uncommitted changes.
It stores commits on the remote for backup.

questions.question: What is git cherry-pick?
questions.correctAnswer: It applies a specific commit from another branch onto the current branch.
wrongAnswers: It selects which files to include in the next commit.
It picks the best branch to merge based on tests.
It removes a specific commit from the history.

questions.question: What is the difference between git reset and git revert?
questions.correctAnswer: reset moves the branch back, rewriting history; revert creates a new commit that undoes another, safe for shared branches.
wrongAnswers: revert rewrites history; reset creates a new undo commit.
reset only affects the remote; revert only affects the local repository.
They are equivalent; revert is the older name of reset.

questions.question: What is the difference between reset --soft, --mixed and --hard?
questions.correctAnswer: --soft keeps changes staged; --mixed keeps them in the working directory; --hard discards everything.
wrongAnswers: --soft discards all changes, --mixed keeps them staged and --hard keeps them in the working directory as unstaged edits.
--soft resets only the remote; --mixed resets local and remote; --hard deletes the branch.
They differ only in speed, not in what happens to the changes.

questions.question: What is git reflog?
questions.correctAnswer: A local log of HEAD movements, useful for recovering "lost" commits.
wrongAnswers: A server-side log of every push made by every collaborator, stored on GitHub and used for auditing access.
A command that reformats commit messages.
A list of files ignored by .gitignore.

questions.question: What is Git Flow?
questions.correctAnswer: A branching strategy with main, develop, feature/*, release/* and hotfix/*.
wrongAnswers: A strategy in which every developer commits directly to main without branches, relying only on feature flags.
GitHub's built-in visual pipeline editor for designing CI/CD flows without writing YAML.
GitHub's built-in CI/CD feature.

questions.question: What is Trunk-Based Development?
questions.correctAnswer: A strategy where everyone integrates frequently into a main branch with short-lived branches and feature flags.
wrongAnswers: A strategy with long-lived feature branches that stay isolated for weeks and are merged only at release time.
A strategy where each developer has a permanent personal branch.
A strategy that forbids feature flags.

questions.question: What is GitHub Flow?
questions.correctAnswer: A simple flow: create a branch from main, commit, open a PR, review, merge and deploy.
wrongAnswers: A flow with long-lived develop, release and hotfix branches in addition to main, with releases merged back into develop.
A visual editor for GitHub Actions workflows.
A process where commits go straight to production without review.

questions.question: What is Conventional Commits?
questions.correctAnswer: A message standard (feat:, fix:, chore:...) that makes changelogs and automated semantic versioning easier.
wrongAnswers: A Git setting that blocks any commit whose message does not reference an existing issue number in the tracker.
A rule that commits must be made at regular intervals.
A Git setting that blocks commits without tests.

questions.question: What is semantic versioning (SemVer)?
questions.correctAnswer: The MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format: major for breaking changes, minor for new features and patch for fixes.
wrongAnswers: The MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format, where major is for bug fixes, minor is for breaking changes and patch is for new backward-compatible features.
A date-based format such as 2024.10.08.
A versioning scheme that increments a single number per commit.

questions.question: What is GitHub Actions?
questions.correctAnswer: An integrated CI/CD platform that runs workflows defined in YAML in response to repository events.
wrongAnswers: A bot that reviews every pull request and approves it automatically when the code style matches the repository's linter rules.
A marketplace for purchasing premium themes and extensions that change how the GitHub interface looks and behaves.
A list of keyboard shortcuts in the GitHub interface.

questions.question: How is a GitHub Actions workflow structured?
questions.correctAnswer: A .github/workflows/*.yml file with on (triggers), jobs, runs-on and steps (commands or reusable actions).
wrongAnswers: A script named workflow in package.json containing the list of shell commands that GitHub runs on every push to main.
A Dockerfile placed in the repository root, which GitHub builds and runs automatically each time a pull request is opened.
A .github/actions.json file with triggers and a single shell script.

questions.question: What are Secrets on GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: Encrypted variables for storing sensitive data (tokens, keys) used in workflows without exposing them in code.
wrongAnswers: Private repositories that only the owner can see.
Hidden branches not shown in the repository list.
Commits that are excluded from the public history.

questions.question: What is CI/CD?
questions.correctAnswer: Continuous Integration (automatic build and tests on every change) and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (automated deploy).
wrongAnswers: Code Inspection and Code Documentation, a manual process where senior developers review and document each change before release.
Continuous Isolation and Continuous Debugging, a practice of keeping every feature in its own branch until it is bug-free.
Continuous Isolation / Continuous Debugging of branches.

questions.question: What are Branch Protection Rules?
questions.correctAnswer: Rules that require PRs, approvals and passing checks, and block force pushes on the branch.
wrongAnswers: Rules that encrypt the contents of a branch so that only its creator and organization owners can read the files.
Rules that automatically delete branches that have not received commits in the last 30 days to keep the repository clean.
Rules that prevent branches from being created.

questions.question: What is CODEOWNERS?
questions.correctAnswer: A file that defines owners for parts of the code, automatically requested as reviewers on PRs.
wrongAnswers: A file listing the legal copyright holders of the repository, required for open source licenses to be valid.
A file that restricts who can clone the repository.
A list of contributors displayed on the repository page.

questions.question: What are Pull Request Templates?
questions.correctAnswer: PR description templates (.github/pull_request_template.md) that standardize the information.
wrongAnswers: Pre-built branches containing common features that can be merged into any repository from the GitHub marketplace.
Repository templates used to generate entirely new repositories with a predefined folder structure and files.
Templates for generating new repositories from scratch.

questions.question: What is a Draft Pull Request?
questions.correctAnswer: A PR marked as a draft, signaling it isn't ready for review or merge yet.
wrongAnswers: A pull request created automatically by Dependabot to update a dependency, which cannot be edited by humans.
A PR that was closed without merging.
A PR created automatically by Dependabot.

questions.question: How do you keep a fork up to date?
questions.correctAnswer: Add the original repository as upstream, run git fetch upstream and merge/rebase, or use "Sync fork" on GitHub.
wrongAnswers: Delete the fork and create a new one every time.
Run git pull origin, since origin always points to the original repository.
Forks update automatically whenever the original changes.

questions.question: What are submodules?
questions.correctAnswer: References to other repositories inside a repository, pinned to a specific commit.
wrongAnswers: Subfolders that Git ignores automatically because they contain generated files, such as build outputs and caches.
Smaller branches created from a feature branch.
npm packages installed inside the repository.

questions.question: What is git bisect?
questions.correctAnswer: A binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug.
wrongAnswers: A command that splits a large commit into two smaller commits interactively, so each one can be reviewed separately.
A command that compares two files or branches side by side in the terminal, highlighting differences line by line.
A command that divides a branch into two new branches.

questions.question: What is git blame?
questions.correctAnswer: It shows who last changed each line of a file and in which commit.
wrongAnswers: It reports which commit broke the build in CI.
It lists users who violated branch protection rules.
It reverts the changes made by a specific author.

questions.question: What is Dependabot?
questions.correctAnswer: A GitHub feature that creates automatic PRs to update dependencies and fix vulnerabilities.
wrongAnswers: A bot that reviews code style and formatting in pull requests, leaving comments when lint rules are violated.
A chatbot for answering questions about a repository.
A tool that removes unused dependencies automatically without PRs.

questions.question: What are GitHub Projects?
questions.correctAnswer: Boards and tables for planning and tracking work, linking issues and PRs.
wrongAnswers: A list of every repository that belongs to an organization, grouped by team and sorted by recent activity.
Separate Git repositories dedicated to documentation, linked to the main repository through submodules.
A list of all repositories belonging to an organization.

questions.question: What is GitHub Discussions?
questions.correctAnswer: A forum inside the repository for questions, ideas and conversations outside of issues.
wrongAnswers: Comment threads attached to individual lines of code in a pull request, used during code review.
A real-time chat for organization members.
A section for reviewing security alerts.

questions.question: How do you sign commits?
questions.correctAnswer: With GPG or SSH (git commit -S), showing the "Verified" badge on GitHub.
wrongAnswers: By adding your name at the end of the commit message.
With git commit --author, which verifies identity.
By enabling 2FA, which signs all commits automatically.

questions.question: How do you revert an already merged PR?
questions.correctAnswer: Use GitHub's "Revert" button, which creates a new PR undoing the changes.
wrongAnswers: Reopen the PR, which automatically undoes the merge.
Delete the source branch, which removes its commits from main.
Use git reset --hard on main and force push, the recommended approach.

questions.question: What is git rebase -i?
questions.correctAnswer: Interactive rebase to reorder, edit, combine (squash) or remove commits.
wrongAnswers: A rebase mode that resolves every conflict automatically by always keeping the version from the target branch.
An incremental rebase that runs in the background and applies commits gradually while you keep working.
A rebase that ignores conflicts automatically.

questions.question: What is --force-with-lease?
questions.correctAnswer: It forces the push only if the remote has no new commits you don't know about, safer than --force.
wrongAnswers: It pushes without running any local Git hooks, which is useful when hooks are slow or failing temporarily.
It forces the push and locks the branch for other collaborators.
It forces the push only on protected branches.

questions.question: How do you remove an already committed sensitive file?
questions.correctAnswer: Rewrite history with git filter-repo or BFG and immediately rotate the exposed credential.
wrongAnswers: Delete the file in a new commit and push it; that removes the content from every previous commit in the history.
Add the file to .gitignore and push; Git then removes it from all previous commits and the credential stays safe.
Make the repository private; the credential is then safe and needs no rotation.

questions.question: What is a reusable workflow (workflow_call)?
questions.correctAnswer: A workflow that can be called by others, avoiding duplicated pipelines across repositories.
wrongAnswers: A workflow that reruns itself automatically when it fails, up to a configured number of attempts.
A workflow that can only be triggered manually from the Actions tab with input parameters.
A workflow cached between runs for speed.

questions.question: What are composite actions?
questions.correctAnswer: Actions that group several steps into one, defined in YAML without needing JavaScript or Docker code.
wrongAnswers: Docker-based actions that compose several containers into one job using docker-compose files.
Actions written in JavaScript that combine multiple repositories.
Actions that run several workflows in parallel.

questions.question: How do you use a matrix strategy in Actions?
questions.correctAnswer: With strategy.matrix to run the same job across several combinations (Node versions, operating systems).
wrongAnswers: With jobs.parallel, which splits a single test file across several runners to finish faster.
With a matrix.yml file at the repository root listing every combination to test.
With on.matrix to trigger workflows on multiple events.

questions.question: How do you speed up workflows?
questions.correctAnswer: Dependency caching (actions/cache), parallel jobs, concurrency to cancel old runs and suitable runners.
wrongAnswers: Run all steps sequentially in a single large job so the runner doesn't need to set up the environment more than once.
Running all steps in a single job sequentially.
Removing tests from CI so builds finish faster.

questions.question: What is concurrency in Actions?
questions.correctAnswer: It ensures that only one run of a group executes at a time and allows canceling previous ones.
wrongAnswers: It runs every job of a workflow at the same time on separate runners, ignoring the needs dependencies between them.
It allows several workflows in different repositories to share the same encrypted secrets and environment variables.
It limits the number of steps per job.

questions.question: What are Environments on GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: Environments (staging, production) with their own secrets, required reviewers and protection rules for deploys.
wrongAnswers: Cloud virtual machines that GitHub provides to developers for writing code in the browser, like Codespaces.
Different branches used for development.
Environment variables defined in .env files in the repository.

questions.question: How do you authenticate Actions to the cloud without static secrets?
questions.correctAnswer: Via OIDC, where GitHub issues short-lived tokens accepted by AWS, Azure and GCP.
wrongAnswers: By using the GITHUB_TOKEN, which is accepted directly by AWS, Azure and GCP as a long-lived cloud credential.
By committing the cloud access keys to a private repository and reading them from the checked-out files during the job.
By storing credentials in the workflow YAML as plain text.

questions.question: What are self-hosted runners?
questions.correctAnswer: Your own machines that execute Actions jobs, useful for specific hardware or private networks, requiring security care.
wrongAnswers: GitHub-managed machines reserved for Enterprise plans, with dedicated hardware and no security considerations for the user.
Containers that GitHub creates automatically inside each repository to run jobs locally on contributors' laptops.
Local copies of workflows that run only on the developer's laptop without GitHub.

questions.question: How do you protect against supply chain attacks in Actions?
questions.correctAnswer: Pin actions by commit SHA, use minimal GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, review dependencies and avoid running code from external PRs with secrets.
wrongAnswers: Always reference actions by the @latest tag so you automatically receive security fixes, and grant write-all permissions to avoid failures.
Allow workflows triggered by external pull requests to access secrets, so that contributions are fully tested before review.
Give GITHUB_TOKEN write-all permissions to avoid failures.

questions.question: What is GITHUB_TOKEN?
questions.correctAnswer: A temporary token automatically generated for each run, with configurable permissions scoped to the repository.
wrongAnswers: A permanent organization-wide token that never expires and has admin access to every repository.
The user's personal access token, shared with every workflow.
A token used only for GitHub Pages deployments.

questions.question: What are Rulesets?
questions.correctAnswer: An evolution of protection rules: they allow rules across multiple repositories, with more flexibility and test modes (evaluate).
wrongAnswers: A set of ESLint and Prettier rules that GitHub enforces automatically on every pull request across the organization.
A list of words and patterns that are banned in issues, discussions and commit messages for moderation purposes.
Rules for formatting commit messages only.

questions.question: What is Merge Queue?
questions.correctAnswer: A queue that tests PRs against the latest version of main before merging, preventing breakage from concurrent merges.
wrongAnswers: A list of pull requests waiting for a reviewer, sorted by creation date, that assigns reviewers in round-robin order.
A feature that postpones all merges until a scheduled release window, such as every Friday afternoon.
A queue that merges PRs in random order to distribute load.

questions.question: What is GitHub Advanced Security?
questions.correctAnswer: A suite with code scanning (CodeQL), secret scanning and dependency review for detecting vulnerabilities.
wrongAnswers: A two-factor authentication method for GitHub accounts.
A firewall that blocks malicious IPs from cloning repositories.
A paid support plan for security incidents.

questions.question: What is CodeQL?
questions.correctAnswer: A static analysis engine that queries code as data to find vulnerabilities.
wrongAnswers: A SQL-like query language for searching issues, pull requests and commits across repositories in the GitHub UI.
A database that stores repository metadata.
A runtime monitoring tool for production apps.

questions.question: What is secret scanning with push protection?
questions.correctAnswer: It detects credentials in commits and blocks the push before the secret reaches the repository.
wrongAnswers: It encrypts any secrets found in commits automatically, so they can stay in the repository without being exposed.
It scans the repository only after a merge and opens an issue a few days later listing the exposed secrets.
It hides secrets from the commit diff in the UI.

questions.question: How do you manage monorepos with GitHub?
questions.correctAnswer: Use CODEOWNERS per folder, workflows with paths filters, tools like Nx/Turborepo and incremental builds with caching.
wrongAnswers: Create a separate GitHub organization for each folder in the monorepo so that permissions are isolated per package.
Run every workflow for every change regardless of path, and avoid CODEOWNERS because it does not support folders.
Avoid CODEOWNERS, since it does not work with monorepos.

questions.question: How do you trigger workflows from external events?
questions.correctAnswer: With repository_dispatch, workflow_dispatch (manual) or webhooks via the API.
wrongAnswers: With the on: external trigger, which listens to any public URL and starts the workflow when it changes.
Only by pushing a commit to the repository, since workflows cannot be started by external systems.
With schedule only, using cron syntax.

questions.question: What are GitHub Apps and OAuth Apps?
questions.correctAnswer: API integrations: GitHub Apps have granular permissions and act per installation; OAuth Apps act on behalf of the user with broad scopes.
wrongAnswers: OAuth Apps have fine-grained permissions and act per installation, while GitHub Apps always act as the user with full account access.
GitHub Apps are mobile applications for iOS and Android, while OAuth Apps are desktop clients that integrate with the Git CLI.
They are the same thing with different names on the marketplace.

questions.question: What are GitHub webhooks?
questions.correctAnswer: HTTP notifications sent to a URL when events occur (push, PR, issue), enabling integrations.
wrongAnswers: Git hooks that run locally before each commit.
Scheduled emails summarizing repository activity.
Browser notifications for new stars on a repository.

questions.question: What is the difference between GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API?
questions.correctAnswer: REST uses multiple fixed endpoints; GraphQL lets you query exactly the needed fields in a single request.
wrongAnswers: GraphQL exposes many fixed endpoints, one per resource, while REST lets you request exactly the fields you need in a single call.
REST can only read data and GraphQL can only write data, so integrations normally use both APIs together.
REST is for public repos and GraphQL for private repos.

questions.question: How does Git store data internally?
questions.correctAnswer: As hash-addressed objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags) in .git/objects, forming an acyclic graph.
wrongAnswers: As a full copy of every file for every commit, in folders named by date.
As diffs stored in a SQLite database inside .git.
As a single compressed JSON file with the whole history.

questions.question: What is a "detached HEAD"?
questions.correctAnswer: A state where HEAD points to a specific commit, not a branch; new commits may be lost if you don't create a branch.
wrongAnswers: A corrupted repository state in which the HEAD file was deleted and Git can no longer determine the current branch.
A state in which the local branch is no longer tracking its remote branch after the remote was renamed or removed.
A state that occurs after a successful merge.

questions.question: What is git worktree?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets you have several working folders of the same repository with different branches simultaneously.
wrongAnswers: It prints the repository's folder tree in the terminal, similar to the tree command, including ignored files.
It displays the repository's folder tree.
It creates a new repository from a subfolder.

questions.question: What is sparse checkout?
questions.correctAnswer: Checking out only part of the repository's files, useful in large monorepos.
wrongAnswers: Cloning only the last commit of the history with --depth 1, which is useful in CI pipelines.
Checking out a branch without its commit history.
Downloading files in parallel to speed up cloning.

questions.question: What is a shallow clone?
questions.correctAnswer: A clone with limited history (--depth 1), faster and lighter, common in CI.
wrongAnswers: A clone that downloads only part of the files in the repository, useful for working on a single folder of a monorepo.
A clone without the .git folder.
A clone that copies only the remote branches.

questions.question: What is Git LFS?
questions.correctAnswer: An extension that stores large files (binaries, media) outside the main repository, keeping only pointers.
wrongAnswers: A Git mode that compresses large binary files inside the repository using a special algorithm, keeping them in .git/objects.
A command that lists the largest files in the history so you can delete them manually with git rm.
A file system for Linux optimized for Git.

questions.question: How do you deal with a very large or slow history?
questions.correctAnswer: Use git gc, shallow clones, partial clone (--filter=blob:none), LFS and remove large files from history.
wrongAnswers: Delete the .git folder and initialize a new repository, since Git cannot handle histories larger than a few gigabytes.
Disable compression with git config core.compression 0, which makes every operation on large histories much faster.
Delete the .git folder and start a new repository.

questions.question: What is git rerere?
questions.correctAnswer: "Reuse recorded resolution": it remembers how you resolved conflicts to reapply them automatically in identical situations.
wrongAnswers: A command that reruns the last failed rebase from the beginning, discarding any conflict resolutions you made.
A command that rewrites remote references so they point to your local branches after a force push.
A command that restores deleted branches.

questions.question: What is a release strategy with maintenance branches?
questions.correctAnswer: Keeping branches like release/1.x to receive fixes (backports via cherry-pick) while development continues on main.
wrongAnswers: Deleting release branches immediately after tagging, since fixes are always shipped only in the next major version.
Creating a new repository for each major version.
Merging every release branch back into main without fixes.

questions.question: How do you automate releases and changelogs?
questions.correctAnswer: With Conventional Commits and tools like semantic-release or release-please, triggered by Actions.
wrongAnswers: Write the changelog manually in each pull request description and copy it into a CHANGELOG file before every release.
Run git log > CHANGELOG.md on a developer's machine and commit the output directly to main before tagging.
By writing the changelog manually in each PR description.

questions.question: How do you configure secure continuous deployment with GitHub Actions?
questions.correctAnswer: Protected environments with approval, OIDC, minimal permissions, reversible deploys (rollback) and required checks before production.
wrongAnswers: Deploy every push from any branch straight to production and skip tests in deploy workflows to reduce the total pipeline time.
Store production credentials as plain text in the workflow YAML so that every job can access them quickly when deploying.
Store production credentials in the repository for quick access.

questions.question: How do you measure the health of an engineering workflow?
questions.correctAnswer: DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore.
wrongAnswers: Counting lines of code written and commits made per developer per day, ranking the team by individual output.
Measuring the number of commits per day per person.
Counting how many stars the repository has.

questions.question: How do you structure governance of a GitHub organization?
questions.correctAnswer: Teams and role-based permissions, SSO/SAML, rulesets, CODEOWNERS, security policies and auditing via the audit log.
wrongAnswers: Use a single shared account for the whole team so that permissions and audit logs are simpler to manage.
Give every member admin access so nobody is blocked.
Rely only on private repositories, with no other controls.
